items.title: From validation trials to clinical reality: implementing AI-supported prostate MRI pathways in the NHS
items.abstract: Prostate cancer remains the most common cancer diagnosed in men in the UK. The adoption of pre-biopsy multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) has improved diagnostic stratification, although it has concurrently increased the burden on radiology services. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for analysing prostate MRIs have demonstrated significant potential in validation tests. Integrating these systems into the NHS will be exceedingly challenging because of concerns around governance, safety, and workflow. This article provides a perspective on AI-assisted prostate MRI and draws on practical experience from pathway design and early implementation planning in a local general hospital. The emphasis is on governance-centric deployment, human-in-the-loop safety, and pathway-level integration rather than the algorithm's performance. AI may support prostate MRI interpretation and improve efficiency within diagnostic pathways; nevertheless, its clinical efficacy is contingent on the quality of its application, rather than only on its validation. Governance-driven pathway design centred on individuals is crucial for ensuring that AI technologies enhance healthcare practices while maintaining safety, equity, and professional autonomy.

items.abstract: Cybersecurity is the core where protection is provided to digital resources like servers, Data centers and Networks. Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) driven cybersecurity strengthens the digital ecosystem. Web Sites and Social media are engines in the modern digital world where organizations, customers and users are facing challenges due to theft of data, money, identity and cyber attacks. Cyber crimes like tampering of digital assets need to be detected with tools and techniques that should be automated. Autonomous Systems in various sectors try to prevent crimes through Anti malware, Antivirus, Firewalls, Encryption and Multi stage authorization. This chapter provides analytical study of various tools, research work carried out with AI techniques. Critical analysis of challenges in unified security frameworks, Models as well as an explainable AI framework for Cybersecurity presented in paper. Quantum Computing capabilities to crack algorithms and decryption of data. Quantum-safe cybersecurity explored along with challenges for the digital world that would arise in future.

items.title: Gated Memory: Admission-Controlled Memory Formation for Conversational AI
items.abstract: Personalized conversational AI relies on long-term memory systems that extract facts from user utterances and store them in persistent vector stores. Despite progress in retrieval, deduplication, and lifecycle management, the formation stage, the moment a fact is first written to storage has received almost no principled attention. We identify this as the binding constraint on memory quality in production systems. Critical contextual signals, such as the distinction between a permanent user attribute and a transient situation, exist only in the original utterance and are irreversibly lost the moment extraction produces a subject-relation-object triple. No downstream process can recover them. We propose Gated Memory, a lightweight, modular formation framework that interposes two decision checkpoints between conversation and storage: an admission gate that evaluates every candidate fact against the full utterance context before extraction runs, and a conditional enrichment stage that grounds admitted facts through an entity scope taxonomy with privacy constraints. The gate evaluates only the current exchange while using prior turns as read-only reference context, and produces a structured formation record. Admitted content is decomposed into atomic facts, each categorized, tagged with provenance (directly stated versus inferred), scoped to its condition of applicability, and grounded in resolved time and place, subject to a constraint that no entity absent from the context may be asserted. On the LoCoMo-10 benchmark with atypical emotional density in utterance data, Gated Memory achieves an overall +2.6% relative improvement in LLM-judge accuracy over a strong baseline with identical retrieval and generation, establishing formation quality as a measurable constraint on memory performance.

items.title: Gauge-Symmetry Knowledge Assembly and Big Knowledge Dynamics: Principles of Artificial Science I
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is approaching a problem that cannot be reduced to the accumulation, retrieval, or representation of knowledge: heterogeneous bodies of knowledge must be assembled so that their local semantics can differ while their deeper structural relations remain operationally compatible. This paper proposes Artificial Science as a framework for this problem. Its central premise is that Integration Scienceidentifies portable mathematical structures across scientific domains, whereas Artificial Science converts such structural portability into executable mechanisms of knowledge transformation, composition, control, and stabilization. We develop the first unified model of this program throughgauge-symmetry knowledge assembly and formulate it as a theory of Big Knowledge Dynamics. The framework begins with a global-to-local geometric architecture in which knowledge contexts form a base space, structural symmetries act on internal representations, and connections, covariant derivatives, curvature, and holonomy govern transport across changing local frames. Within this architecture, four mechanism-specific sectors form a staged knowledge dynamics. provides the minimal model of covariant single-charge knowledge transport; provides a non-Abelian model of internally mediated multi-component assembly; supplies a doublet control architecture for externality-driven state transformation; and spontaneous symmetry breaking together with Higgs-like stabilization provides a model of locally stable yet adaptive rational organization. These sectors are not asserted to be ontologically identical to physical gauge theories. Their role is structural: each supplies a mathematically constrained interface that can be mapped into domain-specific knowledge systems and re-grounded in their own semantics. We combine these mechanisms into a staged assembly operator, ABKD = Sstab ∘ XSU(2) ∘ BSU(3) ∘ TU(1), representing transport, internal binding, externally induced transformation, and stabilization. The model separates representation change from content change, local curvature from global memory, internal mediation from external control, and stability from rigidity. Finally, we formulate a machine-facing layer in which formal objects are translated into computational objects, experimental manipulations, observable metrics, and falsifiable predictions. Gauge symmetry is thereby recast not as an analogy imported from physics but as a candidate structural technology for operational knowledge assembly. Artificial Science is proposed as the science of converting portable deep structures into executable and testable knowledge dynamics.

items.title: General‐purpose agents in human‐machine teams: Can we preserve meaningful human control?
items.abstract: Abstract As General‐Purpose AI (GPAI) grows more capable of cross‐domain reasoning and multi‐agent coordination, it reshapes the design space of military human‐machine teams and introduces new opportunities for adaptability as well as new risks for Meaningful Human Control (MHC). The paper presents an integrated delegation framework for preserving MHC in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams. It combines play‐based task structuring, normative constraints, LLM‐mediated interaction, and an exploratory empirical evaluation with military professionals. Part of this framework is DIALOG, an LLM‐mediated interaction component that translates natural language into doctrine‐aligned plays, and builds up a context with ethical, legal, and operational constraints. We evaluate this framework in TNO's vehicle simulation facility, where five military professionals executed tactical missions using closed play, open play, and goal‐based delegation modes. Findings reveal a nuanced autonomy‐control trade‐off: operators initially favored higher‐autonomy modes but reverted to more structured control when confronted with unexpected or non‐doctrinal agent behaviors. The results highlight implications for MHC, transparency, and trust calibration, and point toward research directions for enhancing tactical competence, communication fidelity, and verifiability in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams.

items.title: Generative AI and learner paradoxes: a paradox theory–based qualitative study in management education
items.abstract: Purpose This study seeks to identify the paradoxes experienced by learners as they use generative artificial intelligence. Design/methodology/approach The present qualitative study uses a two-phase iterative design with member validation approach and paradox theory as the theoretical lens. Drawing on a cross-country sample of 59 participants from four countries – India, Nepal, Zimbabwe and Syria, open-ended essay question responses are recorded. Findings The study identifies five paradoxes, namely competence and convenience paradox, efficiency and dependency paradox, time-saved and time-wasted paradox, productivity and creativity paradox and autonomy and accountability paradox. The various coping mechanisms used by learners to manage these paradoxes have been identified. Originality/value This study provides a useful empirical application of the paradox theory within the management education realm by identifying the paradoxical tensions experienced and various coping strategies used by learners, from their lived experiences in a cross-country context.

items.title: Generative AI as Teacher-Guided Feedback: Exploring Independent Academic Writing among First-Generation Undergraduates in Tamil Nadu
items.abstract: First-generation undergraduates in Tamil Nadu often arrive at college with strong oral reasoning but little prior exposure to the conventions of academic English. Many have studied in Tamil-medium schools, and few have a parent or older sibling who can read a draft and say what is missing. Generative AI tools now offer them a reader at any hour. Yet unmediated use can slide into outsourcing, where the tool writes and the student submits. This article examines a middle path: generative AI positioned as teacher-guided feedback rather than as a text producer. Drawing on a qualitative multiple-case design in [two] arts and science colleges in the Kongu region, we followed [n] first-generation undergraduates across a [12]-week writing module. Teachers set explicit boundaries, modelled feedback-seeking prompts, and required students to keep a revision log showing what they accepted, rejected or reworked. Data came from semi-structured interviews, draft histories, revision logs and teacher reflective notes, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: (1) from answer-seeking to questionasking, (2) the teacher as a trust anchor, (3) language as both bridge and barrier, and (4) the slow growth of evaluative judgement. Students who used the tool within a teacher-framed routine reported greater confidence in planning and revising their own arguments, while teacher mediation appeared central to preventing dependency. The study argues that the pedagogical value of generative AI for first-generation writers lies less in the tool than in the feedback culture built around it. Implications are offered for writing instruction, institutional AI policy and bilingual support in regional Indian higher education

items.title: Generative AI in Fashion Design Education
items.abstract: This chapter covers the transformative role of artificial intelligence in fashion design education, with particular attention to the creation of a framework for prompt literacy utilizing generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Midjourney, and Newarc AI. This chapter also examines how second-year students in Amity University Kolkata's fashion design and fashion communication department generate virtual rapid clothing prototypes of their designs and develop print motifs using AI-powered tools, especially generative AI, which ultimately enhances the significance of these tools for the changing fashion landscape. Participants have created artwork in a variety of mediums, including Mahbubani art, terracotta, ceramics, and print motifs inspired by seashells, insect using mandalas art, Persian carpets, and other subjects like “Joy in Simplicity” and “The Harmony of Nature and Feminine Grace”. The AI-Augmented Fashion Design Education Framework (AI-AFDEF) was emphasized in this book chapter's discussion of traditional versus tech-driven approaches.

items.title: Generative AI Steering and Human Authoring: Complementary Search-as-Learning Scaffolds in Cross-Session Aggregated Academic Search
items.abstract: Aggregated academic search interfaces combine resources from heterogeneous sources, such as scholarly libraries and reference encyclopedias, into a single workspace. Such tasks frequently span multiple sessions, requiring learners to return to and resume work after hours or days. End-of-session consolidation, the activity of organizing and synthesizing gathered information so it can be resumed later, is important in this setting but underexplored in search-as-learning. Generative AI (GenAI) has the potential to make consolidation more efficient, but it may also shift cognitive work away from the learner. This study compares two consolidation scaffolds embedded in the workspace framework of an existing academic search interface that aggregates and clusters saved search results from two different sources (our university library and Wikipedia), which was developed in earlier work. STAIS (Steerable AI Summaries) provides a workspace enhancement that produces GenAI summaries that users can correct, reorganize, and fact-check, automating parts of the consolidation activity. NT (Note-Taking) provides a workspace enhancement that includes rich-text note editors that learners can use to author their own consolidations of what they have found. In a controlled between-subjects study (n=36), participants completed two sessions one week apart while searching an unfamiliar topic using either STAIS or NT. The two conditions produced contrasting post-resumption outcome profiles: STAIS supported faster task resumption and was associated with broader conceptual coverage and higher self-reported domain knowledge, whereas NT was associated with richer inter-concept connections and higher self-reported certainty.

items.title: Generative AI use and the 2022–2025 decline in PISA performance across countries
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has spread rapidly among students since 2022, and PISA 2025 recorded its lowest results. In a preregistered study, we related four independent country-level AI-use measures to the mathematics, reading and science PISA performance of 15-year-olds. Countries with more AI use scored higher, but, critically, they also tended to show larger declines or smaller gains between 2022 and 2025, as predicted. This association was no longer detectable after adjusting for 2018 performance, before generative AI existed. AI use was unrelated to change from 2015 to 2018, but some measures were associated with declines from 2018 to 2022, during the pandemic, mainly in mathematics. The spread of country means, stable since 2015, narrowed by 7–9% from 2022 to 2025, as upper-middle performers lost and some low performers, which tend to use AI less, gained relative ground. These patterns suggest AI may have contributed to the recent decline.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Human Creativity: Revisiting the Normative Foundations of Intellectual Property
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (gen-AI) undermines the traditional foundations of intellectual property (IP) law by challenging long-standing assumptions about creative production. Historically, copyright and patent systems were based on identifiable human creators whose work, talent, character, and intentionality deserved legal protection. However, gen-AI systems, which can generate text, images, music, software code, and other creative outputs, complicate these assumptions. This article contends that gen-AI does not raise new doctrinal issues but instead reveals deeper conflicts within the normative underpinnings of IP law. The article proposes a human-centred IP framework that preserves meaningful protection for human creative agency while recognising the collective nature of creativity in technologically mediated societies. Drawing on labour, personality, utilitarian, and democratic culture theories, it demonstrates how AI disrupts the relationship between human creativity and IP protection. The article first examines the philosophical foundations of IP law, then analyses how gen-AI disrupts traditional concepts of authorship, originality, and creative agency, evaluates potential normative responses, and proposes a human-centred framework for regulating technologically mediated creativity.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in oncology patient counselling: Transforming oncology pharmacy practice through human–AI collaborative care
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To critically evaluate the current evidence regarding the application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in oncology patient counselling, with particular emphasis on oncology pharmacy practice, and to distinguish direct oncology evidence from indirect evidence derived from general healthcare and other digital-health technologies. DATA SOURCES: PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science were searched for relevant literature published from January 2020 through August 2026, with the final search conducted in August 2026. Search terms included combinations of terms related to generative artificial intelligence, large language models, ChatGPT, GPT, Med-PaLM, oncology, cancer, patient counselling, patient education, medication counselling, medication adherence, symptom monitoring, toxicity monitoring, telepharmacy, and digital health. Reference lists of relevant publications were also examined to identify additional relevant literature. DATA SUMMARY: The identified literature demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in artificial intelligence technologies, clinical settings, populations, and outcomes. Evidence directly evaluating GenAI in oncology patient education and counselling remains limited but suggests potential applications in patient education, healthcare communication, information simplification, and selected supportive-care functions. Evidence from general healthcare populations and from conventional chatbots, telehealth, remote monitoring, and other non-generative digital-health technologies provides contextual but indirect support. Evidence for GenAI-specific improvements in medication adherence, toxicity recognition, hospitalization outcomes, accessibility, workflow efficiency, and continuity of care remains insufficient. The review also identified important concerns regarding hallucinations, accuracy, bias, privacy, accountability, and the need for professional oversight. A pharmacist-supervised human-AI collaborative framework is proposed as a conceptual model based on the reviewed evidence, existing AI governance principles, and oncology-pharmacy considerations. CONCLUSIONS: GenAI represents a potentially useful adjunct to oncology patient counselling, particularly for patient education and communication. However, current evidence does not establish its clinical effectiveness across major oncology-pharmacy outcomes. Findings from non-generative digital-health technologies should not be interpreted as direct evidence for GenAI. Prospective oncology-specific studies are needed to evaluate clinical effectiveness, patient-centred outcomes, medication-related outcomes, safety, usability, and implementation feasibility. Until stronger evidence is available, GenAI should complement rather than replace oncology pharmacist-led counselling and clinical decision-making.

items.title: Giving the Emperor clothes: operationalizing AI ethics principles in corporations
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies raise enormous questions for society and how we should live. For corporations, AI raises questions about how organizations ought to incorporate principles and other forms of ethical guidance into their work. The movement from theory to practice, or “the operationalization question” demands that organizations not only have good intentions, but actual institutionalized approaches towards ethical problem solving. In this paper, we look at the movement from theory to practice, and particularly at the use of principles as a way to guide ethical behavior, considering, first, why implementation of principles is difficult, second, how to move from abstract principles to actionable principles, and third, illustrating this progression through seven real-life AI cases. These seven cases each relate to an ethical principle: (1) protecting human dignity and rights, and the International Baccalaureate exam replacement by algorithm, (2) promoting human well-being, and Amazon warehouse worker injuries, (3) investing in humanity, and the Partnership on AI’s work to bring together AI corporations and civil society, (4) promoting inclusion, and IBM’s response to the Gender Shades study, (5) protecting the environment, and Hugging Face’s tracking AI energy use, (6) maintaining accountability, and the Christchurch, New Zealand mass shooting response by Facebook and Western Digital, (7) and, lastly, promoting transparency, and AI model cards. The cases model the movement from abstract principle to concrete action, and collectively illustrate a pattern that can be repeated in many contexts, thus demonstrating a new possible solution for organizations implementing ethics.

items.title: GlucoPRISM: Protocol-Supervised Pretraining for Cross-Cohort Glucose Transfer
items.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models encode each day as one vector that mixes who the person is, what happened that day and how the sensor measured it, so measurement differences travel with the representation into new cohorts. We ask whether pretraining can place the measurement component that harms transfer in known coordinates, so that deployment drops them with a fixed projection and no target data. GlucoPRISM supervises a GlucoFM backbone with response contracts, rules for how each part of the representation should change when only the day or only the sensor changes: a 64-dimensional Trait band should change with neither, a 48-dimensional State band only across days, and a 16-dimensional Sensor band should track the device. Synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired Dexcom and Libre recordings, different-day pairs and glucose-summary targets supply this supervision without clinical labels. Across twelve cross-cohort directions, dropping the Sensor band from the same frozen encoder raises mean transfer AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57, against 69.3 for GlucoFM. The gain has two parts. Into CGMacros, the one target cohort recorded with two sensor types, filtering adds 11 to 19 points, and this holds when the generator is recalibrated on half of the participants and scored on the other half. On the other eight directions filtering is neutral and the encoder itself exceeds GlucoFM by 3.5 points. The device remains linearly decodable after filtering, so the filter removes a device-related component that harms transfer rather than all measurement information. The retained bands improve window AUROC on thirteen of fourteen public task--cohort cells (Holm-adjusted p=0.031) and correlation on fourteen of fifteen clinical endpoints in an external cohort of 9,303 participants.

items.title: GOVERNANÇA DA INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL NA SAÚDE: DESAFIOS PARA O MONITORAMENTO DE VIESES, ERROS ALGORÍTMICOS E SEGURANÇA DO PACIENTE
items.abstract: OBJETIVO: Analisar os desafios da governança da IA na saúde, com ênfase no monitoramento de vieses, na identificação de erros algorítmicos e na segurança do paciente. MÉTODOS: Revisão narrativa da literatura, de abordagem qualitativa e caráter descritivo-analítico. A busca contemplou a Biblioteca Virtual em Saúde, incluindo LILACS e MEDLINE, além da SciELO e PubMed. Foram utilizados os descritores DeCS/MeSH Inteligência Artificial (Artificial Intelligence), Segurança do Paciente (Patient Safety), Algoritmos (Algorithms), Gestão de Riscos (Risk Management) e Sistemas de Apoio à Decisão Clínica (Decision Support Systems, Clinical), combinados pelos operadores booleanos AND e OR. Dos oito documentos avaliados, sete artigos publicados entre 2025 e 2026 foram incluídos, submetidos à leitura integral e interpretação crítica. RESULTADOS: A baixa representatividade das bases de treinamento e as diferenças de desempenho entre grupos populacionais constituíram fatores associados aos vieses algorítmicos. Foram identificados riscos de falsos negativos, alertas clínicos inadequados e deterioração do desempenho dos modelos após sua implantação. A indefinição das responsabilidades institucionais e a insuficiência de mecanismos de monitoramento dificultam a identificação e correção dessas falhas. No SUS, a fragmentação dos registros clínicos, as desigualdades tecnológicas e as limitações da formação profissional representam obstáculos adicionais à supervisão dos sistemas inteligentes. CONCLUSÃO: A governança da IA requer validação local, auditorias periódicas, indicadores de equidade e supervisão humana contínua. A pesquisa identifica requisitos técnicos, éticos e institucionais para o monitoramento dos algoritmos, contribuindo para a organização de mecanismos de prevenção de riscos assistenciais e responsabilização pelas decisões clínicas.

items.title: GPT-4o Translation of Pediatric Discharge Instructions Across Languages
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Patients and caregivers who use languages other than English in health care settings rarely receive language-concordant discharge instructions. Large language models show promise for improving access to translations but must be validated to ensure their output is safe for clinical use. This study measured the quality of GPT-4o medical translations to Portuguese, Haitian Creole, and Arabic. METHODS: Previously translated personalized discharge instructions (performed by professional human translators) were extracted from inpatient admissions at a large US pediatric academic medical center. The discharge instructions were translated to Portuguese, Haitian Creole, and Arabic by GPT-4o. Medical translators then evaluated the translations using both the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework and a preference scale. RESULTS: Translations of 14 to 20 discharge instructions for each of the 3 languages were evaluated. Noninferiority testing showed no significant difference in translation quality between GPT-4o and human translations for Portuguese and Arabic, but worse performance by GPT-4o than human translations for Haitian Creole (mean MQM score 90.5 ± SD 5.5 vs 97.0 ± SD 2.1). Linguists preferred the human translation over GPT-4o in 69% (SE = 7%) of the Haitian Creole cases. CONCLUSIONS: In this cross-sectional study, GPT-4o translation performance of pediatric discharge instructions was noninferior for Portuguese and Arabic but was worse in Haitian Creole. Human validation of medical translations remains necessary for all languages, but large language models can be used to draft high-quality translations in languages with proven high performance, while resources are shifted toward more intensive post-editing of translations in languages with lower performance.

items.title: Grounding language models with deterministic verifiers for fraud detection
items.abstract: Abstract Financial fraud detection is complicated by severe class imbalance, temporal change, adversarial manipulation, and the need for evidence-grounded explanations. Although large language models can generate readable rationales, their claims may be unsupported when they are not independently checked against structured evidence. We propose VR-FraudNet, a five-stage framework combining a time-conditioned spectral graph encoder, LightGBM triage and threshold routing, a schema-constrained rationale language model, a fixed deterministic verifier, and an isotonic probability mixer with split-conformal calibration. The language model proposes machine-checkable claims for review-band transactions, while the verifier evaluates each claim against the available transaction, temporal, and graph evidence. Verifier-rejected rationales are excluded from automated use, and the corresponding transactions are assigned to human-review escalation. D1 BAF, D2 AMLworld HI-Small, and D3 IEEE-CIS are used as the primary predictive benchmarks, whereas D4 Elliptic++ and D5 DGraph-Fin support complementary temporal-graph, strict-inductive, temporal-robustness, and message-passing stress tests. VR-FraudNet improves AUPRC over TabTransformer from 0.5012 to 0.5247 on D1, from 0.5137 to 0.5824 on D2, and from 0.7234 to 0.7456 on D3. The predeclared 5-percentage-point temporal-degradation target is satisfied in the evaluated D1 month-drift, D3 late-fold, and D4 pre-shock comparisons. However, D4 post-shock AUPRC decreases from 0.6823 to 0.6087, an absolute reduction of 7.36 percentage points that exceeds the target. Under the four-family structured predictive edit set, mean evasion rates are 0.0667, 0.1016, and 0.1672 for budgets 1, 2, and 4, respectively. Under the stated operational cost assumptions, VR-FraudNet produces lower total loss than TabTransformer, with the largest difference on D2. Measured p99 latency is 10.23 ms on the common path and 175.23 ms on the escalation path under the reported hardware configuration. Empirical split-conformal miscoverage remains below the stated bounds in the reported calibration settings, while the formal marginal-coverage statement applies only under the stated exchangeability assumptions. These findings support verifier-grounded fraud detection under the evaluated public datasets and protocols but do not establish universal adversarial safety, temporal robustness, regulatory sufficiency, or deployment readiness.

items.title: GRPODropout: Less is More for Online Reinforcement Learning Rollouts
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) methods such as GRPO substantially improve large language model reasoning but often suffer from policy entropy collapse: the loss of sampling diversity weakens exploration and limits further improvement. Existing methods address this issue either through algorithm-level interventions, such as reward modification and entropy/KL regularization, or through token-level reweighting. We investigate a complementary perspective: entropy collapse can also be mitigated by changing which generated rollouts contribute to policy updates. Under the same sampling budget, not all rollouts contribute positively to an update, and selectively excluding some can improve learning. To address this, we propose GRPODropout: before the standard update, we use a simple strategy that selectively removes a small number of high-probability positive-advantage rollouts and recenters the retained advantages. To motivate this design, we develop a rollout-level theoretical analysis that guides method design and threshold selection. The method changes only rollout usage, and adds negligible computational overhead. Experiments show higher accuracy than original GRPO and higher actor entropy while using fewer rollout samples for updates, illustrating "less is more." This work provides insight into RL rollout usage: removing some rollouts can improve performance. Code is available at https://github.com/hexuandeng/GRPODropout/.

items.title: Guideline adherence and expert-rated potential safety concerns in AI-generated dietary advice for patients with cirrhosis: a comparative evaluation of large language models
items.abstract: Background Patients with cirrhosis require complication-specific nutritional counseling. Large language models are increasingly used for health information seeking, but the guideline adherence and potential safety concerns of their dietary advice for cirrhosis remain uncertain. Methods Thirty-six standardized simulated cases represented compensated cirrhosis, cirrhosis with ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy recovery. Each case was submitted once to DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Qwen, and Claude through their official web interfaces, generating 144 English-language recommendations. Three reviewers performed de novo model-blinded assessments using a locked framework. The primary outcome was response-level Guideline Adherence; secondary outcomes included Error Count, Any Major Error, and Harm Flag. Results Mean Guideline Adherence was 7.00 ± 0.00 for ChatGPT, 6.97 ± 0.17 for Claude, 6.94 ± 0.19 for DeepSeek, and 6.44 ± 0.84 for Qwen (Friedman p < 0.001). In hepatic encephalopathy recovery, Qwen scored 5.36 ± 0.54 and was lower than each other model after Holm adjustment (all adjusted p = 0.009). Any Major Error occurred in 0 ChatGPT, 2 Claude, 4 DeepSeek, and 11 Qwen responses; corresponding Harm Flag counts were 0, 1, 2, and 8. Most events occurred during hepatic encephalopathy recovery and involved protein-related recommendations. Conclusion Under standardized English-language structured prompting, all four models generally reproduced core cirrhosis nutrition principles. However, Qwen showed lower adherence and more frequent protein-related errors in hepatic encephalopathy recovery. Expert verification remains necessary before patient-facing or individualized use.

items.title: Hacia un Modelo de Intervención para la Preparación Física y Mental que Mejore el Rendimiento de los E-Sport en Colombia
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to understand the elements that shape physical and mental preparation in esports in Colombia and, based on their interpretation, to propose a model aimed at optimizing competitive performance while promoting players' overall health and well-being. The research adopted a qualitative approach with a hermeneutic orientation. The methodological strategies included in-depth interviews with professional players, coaches, and esports experts, participant observation conducted over four weeks with the esports team of the Industrial University of Santander, and a review of the relevant scientific literature. Data were analyzed through open, axial, and selective coding, allowing the identification of emerging categories and the establishment of relationships between empirical findings and theoretical knowledge. The results revealed that physical and mental preparation are essential components of competitive performance, contributing to improved concentration, endurance, emotional regulation, injury prevention, and decision-making under pressure. Furthermore, the findings highlighted the need for an interdisciplinary model integrating physical training, psychological preparation, ergonomics, nutrition, and professional monitoring to strengthen training processes and support the sustainable development of esports in Colombia.

items.title: Harnessing Machine Learning for Ultrafast Science in Facility Settings: Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: Ultrafast science is rapidly evolving from a collection of specialized laser experiments into a facility-scale, data-intensive research endeavour. High-repetition-rate femtosecond and attosecond sources, synchronized multidimensional diagnostics, and increasingly nonlinear laser-matter interactions now generate heterogeneous data streams whose volume, speed, and complexity often exceed the capacity of conventional manual workflows. This chapter examines how machine learning can become an enabling layer for next-generation ultrafast facilities, with emphasis on the Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) ecosystem. We discuss the scientific drivers for artificial-intelligence-assisted experimentation, propose a facility-scale digital architecture spanning acquisition, ingestion, storage, analytics, machine learning, adaptive feedback, and user interfaces, and review representative examples from ELI ALPS, ELI Beamlines, and ELI-NP. The central thesis is that machine learning should not be treated merely as an offline data-analysis tool; rather, when constrained by physical insight and embedded in robust data infrastructure, it can support real-time diagnostics, surrogate modeling, anomaly detection, experimental optimization, and progressively autonomous discovery workflows.

items.title: Helping Oneself by Helping a Rival: Social-Media Platforms’ Policies on Enabling Features for Influencers
items.abstract: Social-media platforms and influencers are often seen as collaborators. However, both rely primarily on advertising services, introducing a competitive dimension to their relationship. As the dominant players in this relationship, platforms have used design features, which they control, to manage this dynamic. Some platforms have adopted an antagonistic approach by disabling certain features (e.g., clickable shopping-related hyperlinks) for influencers, while others take a more cooperative stance, allowing influencers to use these features for free or for a fee. We develop a game-theoretic model to explore the competition between the two parties and study the platform’s decision to enable or disable a feature that enhances the effectiveness and efficiency of an influencer’s service. We show that even when the platform cannot charge the influencers for using the feature, it can still benefit if the advertisers' valuation of the platform's service is not significantly lower than that of the influencer's service. While enabling the feature may result in a loss of market share, the platform can potentially offset this loss by raising its prices. Enhancing the influencer’s effectiveness can benefit the platform, but efficiency improvements alone never do, highlighting that the platform's benefit from helping the influencer depends on the nature and extent of the support. A win–win situation for the platform and the influencer may come at the expense of some advertisers, suggesting the platform’s helping the influencer can lead to a “collusive” outcome, despite the competition for advertisers. If the platform can charge a fee for using the feature, it should always enable the feature at an appropriate fee, as this will benefit the platform. The additional fee revenue may come with no change in the platform’s advertising revenue, with an increase in the advertising revenue, or at the expense of some advertising revenue. The platform strategically uses the fee to influence the influencer’s service offering, which affects the platform’s revenue mix under the new business model.

items.title: HISA: An End-to-End Smartphone-Mediated Channel for Remote Airflow Actuation
items.abstract: Remote communication is predominantly audiovisual and rarely allows bodily action at one location to produce a physical effect elsewhere. We present HISA (Haptic Interaction via Smartphone-mediated Airflow), an end-to-end system that captures intentional blowing through a smartphone microphone, derives a relative intensity sequence, transmits it, and replays it through a remote pump-and-nozzle actuator. Three studies examined user-to-phone distance, correspondence between human-generated and reproduced airflow under three mapping strategies, and feasibility in a candle-extinguishing task. HISA preserved temporal intensity profiles more consistently than absolute airflow magnitude and produced consequential effects on a remote object. A separate cross-city vignette illustrated geographically distributed operation. These findings establish the technical feasibility of the sensing–transmission–actuation pipeline but do not demonstrate mediated social touch or improvements in social presence, connectedness, affect, or communication quality. HISA provides a foundation for future development and controlled dyadic evaluation of remote airflow interaction.

items.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer
items.abstract: Objective: Prostate cancer, one of the most common cancers affecting men’s health worldwide, ranks second among cancer-related deaths. Therefore, it represents a critical health issue, and early diagnosis is crucial. Several imaging and analytical methods are used to diagnose this condition. Materials and Methods: This study focuses on research conducted between 2021 and 2025 that analyzes, diagnoses, and grades prostate cancer based on histopathological images using machine learning and deep learning algorithms. In this context, the reviewed studies also include an analysis of findings related to preprocessing and feature extraction methods that may aid in prostate cancer detection, as well as the classifiers used. Results: According to the findings of the reviewed studies, artificial intelligence-supported prostate cancer detection systems demonstrate high clinical performance and significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy of pathologists by enabling rapid diagnosis. The presented research findings indicate a need for comprehensive studies focusing on prostate cancer using histopathological images. Conclusion: The integration of artificial intelligence is transforming prostate cancer pathology from a traditional and subjective process into a data-driven and standardized framework. This systematic analysis of histopathological images will make significant contributions to future prostate cancer research, help achieve more reliable results in clinical decision-making processes, and lay the groundwork for personalized medicine.

items.title: How to define the normativity of techniques in the era of the Capitalocene and surveillance?
items.abstract: The article examines how to define the normativity of technologies in the era of the Capitalocene and surveillance capitalism, starting from the observation that the capitalist economy is responsible for a systematic destruction of living spaces—economic, mental, social, and political. To name this process, the author mobilizes the concept of ecofragmentation, inspired by Baptiste Morizot, and proposes rethinking technology on the basis of what Gilbert Simondon calls alimentation, understood as the articulation between means, ends, energy, materials, and human motives. The text analyzes surveillance capitalism as a sociotechnical system that structurally depends on invisibilized human labor, particularly commercial content moderation. Drawing on the case of women and men workers in the Global South, the author argues that this labor consists in assuming psychological trauma “for others,” thereby displacing norms of life and instituting a division of affective and perceptual labor. Added to this is the materiality of the digital, marked by extractivist mining practices and the exploitation of human and nonhuman populations. Building on the Simondonian concept of the transindividual, the article argues that thinking about “technologies of the future” requires forming collectives with those who materially and symbolically produce the technical world.

items.title: How to post-train on a surrogate: Envelope sampling mitigates reward hacking
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly post-trained against LLM judges and other cheap surrogates because the true reward, such as human preference, is too expensive to query at scale. This practice often leads to reward hacking, where reinforcement learning against a miscalibrated surrogate leads to undesirable side effects. In this work, we study a setting in which a small number $n$ of model outputs are annotated with ground-truth labels (e.g., from expert review) and used to recalibrate the LLM judge before optimizing against it. Prior approaches to judge recalibration are costly or heuristic, and it is known that on-policy sampling fails when the surrogate is miscalibrated on a rare set of outputs. In this work, we propose envelope sampling, a theoretically-grounded method for judge recalibration that seeks to minimize an upper bound on the regret of the post-trained model under the assumption that the human reward and re-calibrated reward lie in an $L^2$ ball around the judge. We give practical algorithms to sample from the envelope by rejection or by fine-tuning against a modified reward, and experiments on clinical note generation and on a controlled sycophancy task show that recalibrating on envelope samples mitigates reward hacking where recalibrating on base-model samples does not.

items.title: How Users Engage With ChatGPT
items.abstract: This chapter examines the prompting practices of three ChatGPT users in academic and professional contexts. Using collaborative autoethnography, the study analyzed interaction histories and reflective narratives from the co-authors. Four shared strategies were identified: directive, constraint-setting, contextualized, and iterative prompting. Information-seeking, transformation, refinement, and verification also appeared as related practices. These practices were interpreted through communicative specification, contextual alignment, and reflective regulation. Over time, the authors moved from loosely structured prompting toward purposeful, contextualized, iterative, and role-shaped interaction. This development was influenced by unsuitable responses, experimentation, revision, and growing awareness of academic and professional demands. The chapter presents prompt literacy as a situated and developing capacity requiring users to direct, evaluate, revise, and verify AI-generated content.

items.title: HowArtificial Intelligence Will Pay Your Subsistence
items.abstract: This essay examines the proposition articulated in the source video essay Como a Inteligência Artificial Vai Pagar Sua Subsistência (How Artificial Intelligence Will Pay Your Subsistence), which argues that artificial intelligence may soon enable a largely autonomous economic production system whose dividends could replace labor income as the material basis of household subsistence. Treating the video as its primary object of analysis, the essay reconstructs its argument into eight propositions and evaluates them in relation to the economics of automation, post-work political theory, and the political economy of distribution. Three research questions organize the inquiry: (1) under what technological and institutional conditions could production become sufficiently autonomous to approximate the system described in the video; (2) why, and through which institutional mechanisms, would the owners of autonomous capital have incentives to share its surplus with the broader population; and (3) what would happen to bargaining power, individual freedom, and social stability during a transition in which automation advances faster than redistribution. The analysis produces four principal findings. First, the vision of autonomous production is economically and technologically coherent in principle, but it is highly contingent in practice. It should therefore be understood not as an inevitable consequence of technological progress, but as an institutional configuration shaped by ownership structures, property rights, taxation, corporate governance, and political decisions. Second, the redistribution anticipated by the video has a recognizable functional logic. If automation substantially reduces the role of labor while production capacity continues to expand, maintaining aggregate demand may require mechanisms capable of distributing purchasing power beyond conventional wage employment. However, historical and comparative evidence suggests that the decisive mechanism is more likely to be public policy than voluntary corporate benevolence. Third, the most consequential risks are political rather than purely technological. A society in which productive capital becomes increasingly autonomous could weaken labor's traditional sources of bargaining power, including the ability to withdraw labor, change employers, or negotiate collectively. It could also create forms of income that are conditional, programmable, politically revocable, or dependent on centralized technological infrastructures. The transition itself may represent the greatest danger, particularly if mass automation occurs years or decades before effective redistribution institutions are established. Fourth, the central question is not whether artificial intelligence can generate abundance, but how the ownership and distribution of that abundance are constitutionally and politically organized. The same technological capacity could contribute either to unprecedented material freedom or to unprecedented economic dependence. Autonomous machines do not determine the political structure of the society in which they operate. Ownership, institutional checks and balances, democratic accountability, and the legal status of the social dividend determine whether automation becomes a mechanism of emancipation or a new architecture of dependency. The essay concludes by proposing institutional design principles for a post-labor transition, emphasizing broad participation in productive capital, predictable and legally protected distribution mechanisms, limits on discretionary control over basic income, democratic oversight of highly autonomous productive systems, and institutional safeguards against excessive concentration of economic and political power. Under these conditions, artificial intelligence could contribute not merely to the substitution of human labor, but to a transition toward a society in which technological productivity expands the material conditions of human autonomy rather than diminishing them.

items.title: Human adaptation to workplace technological change: Digital skill-development needs, training alignment, and job satisfaction in Europe
items.abstract: Rapid workplace digitalisation is intensifying employees’ skill-adjustment demands, making the alignment between technological change, learning opportunities, and worker wellbeing increasingly important. This study examines human adaptation to workplace technological change by analysing how substantial digital skill-development needs without recent job-related training, job-related training, and the alignment of training content with technology-induced skill demands are associated with job satisfaction in Europe. The analysis uses anonymised microdata from the 2021 Cedefop European Skills and Jobs Survey, applying survey-weighted OLS models with individual and employment controls, country, occupation and industry fixed effects, country-clustered standard errors, and wild-cluster bootstrap robustness tests. Employees who simultaneously reported moderate or great digital skill-development needs and no recent job-related training reported 0.341 points lower job satisfaction (β = −0.341, p < 0.001). Among workers with comparable substantial needs, training participation was associated with 0.382 points higher satisfaction (β=0.382, p<0.001). The interaction between digital skill-development need and technology-targeted training was positive (β=0.211, p=0.001; bootstrap p=0.014), indicating an increasing relative advantage over generic training. The targeted-versus-generic difference shifted from −0.247 points at no need to +0.176 at moderate need and +0.387 at great need, supporting an adaptive-alignment mechanism.

items.title: Human Ancestry, Slavery and Reparative Justice
items.abstract: A speculative reflection on survival, historical acknowledgment and responsibility for repair. Could people alive today be, in part, the descendants of historical wrongdoers whose coercion and access to resources helped their lineages survive? This reflective essay examines that hypothesis without equating reproductive success with moral worth. It distinguishes genealogical descent from genetic inheritance and considers violence, cooperation, care, mixed ancestry and chance. It then applies these distinctions to transatlantic slavery, historical acknowledgment and reparative justice. The central argument rejects inherited personal guilt while recognising that institutional continuity, retained benefits and unresolved injuries can ground present responsibilities. Moral responsibility and enforceable legal liability are considered separately, alongside the evidence, participation and fairness needed to design reparative programmes. This essay developed from questions and reflections by Agostinho NP da Silva, with drafting, research support and editorial assistance from ChatGPT (OpenAI). It is a referenced reflective essay and has not undergone external peer review. Its moral arguments are interpretations, and its hypothetical examples are illustrative. The edition includes 17 references and is provided in PDF, EPUB and editable HTML formats under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

items.title: Human-Centered AI and Decision Support in Security Operations Centers
items.abstract: The growing complexity of cyber threats has made Security Operations Centers (SOCs) essential for real-time threat detection, incident response, and infrastructure protection. However, traditional black-box AI models often reduce trust and transparency in cybersecurity decisions. This chapter explores human-centered Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for improving interpretable threat detection, anomaly analysis, risk prioritization, and analyst decision-making. It also presents an AIoT-based “Explainable Intelligent SOC Monitoring System for Smart Enterprise Networks” integrating IoT network sensors, edge devices, AI intrusion detection, SHAP and LIME explainability, federated learning, and adaptive alert prioritization. A real-time SOC dashboard provides attack explanations, threat scores, and response support. Human–AI collaboration, analyst feedback, fairness, bias mitigation, trust, accountability, and regulatory concerns are also discussed to support more transparent, reliable, and trustworthy cyber defense systems.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration in Digital Marketing: Evidence from an Emerging Economy, Somalia
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping digital marketing through automation, customer analytics, personalization, and data-driven decision-making. However, empirical evidence on human–AI collaboration in emerging and fragile economies remains limited. This study examined the adoption of human–AI collaboration in digital marketing among businesses in Somalia, identified key barriers to AI adoption, and assessed the association between human–AI collaboration and customer engagement, marketing efficiency, and business growth. The study used a positivist research approach and a quantitative cross-sectional survey design. Data were collected from 86 business owners, marketing managers, digital marketing specialists, and ICT/technology officers using purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Spearman's rank correlation, and multiple linear regression. Respondents reported frequent use of AI-assisted content creation, customer analytics, marketing automation, social media management, and AI-supported decision-making. The principal barriers were limited technical skills, limited infrastructure, implementation costs, data privacy concerns, and organizational resistance to change. Spearman's correlations indicated positive associations between human–AI collaboration and customer engagement (ρ = .684), marketing efficiency (ρ =.725), and business growth (ρ = .658), all reported at p < .001. Regression models explained 50.7% of the variance in customer engagement, 54.9% in marketing efficiency, and 46.4% in business growth. Human–AI collaboration was positively associated with each outcome after controlling for organizational size and industry sector. Because the study is cross-sectional and based on a purposive sample, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The results highlight the importance of combining AI capabilities with human judgment, creativity, contextual knowledge, and responsible data practices in Somalia's digital marketing environment.

items.title: Human, AI, and Hybrid Ensembles for Detection of Adaptive, RL-based Social Bots
items.abstract: The use of reinforcement learning to dynamically adapt and evade detection is now well-documented in several cybersecurity settings including Covert Social Influence Operations (CSIOs), in which bots try to spread disinformation. While AI bot detectors have improved greatly, they are largely limited to detecting static bots that do not adapt dynamically. We present the first systematic study comparing the ability of humans, AI models, and hybrid Human-AI ensembles in detecting adaptive bots powered by reinforcement learning (RL) . Using data from a controlled, IRB-approved, five-day experiment with participants interacting on a social media platform infiltrated by RL-trained bots spreading disinformation to influence participants on 4 topics, we examine factors potentially shaping human detection capabilities: demographic characteristics, temporal learning effects, social network position, engagement patterns, and collective intelligence mechanisms. We first test 13 hypotheses comparing human bot detection performance against 6 state-of-the-art AI bot detectors — 2 that use traditional machine learning and 4 that use large language models. We investigate several aggregation strategies that combine human reports of bots with AI predictions, as well as retraining protocols that leverage human supervision. Our findings challenge intuitive assumptions about bot detection, reveal unexpected patterns in how humans identify bots, and show that combining human bot reports with AI predictions outperforms humans alone and AI alone. We conclude with a discussion of the practical implications of these results for industry.

items.title: Hygiene and industrial safety education in Algeria: An assessment of university curriculum and student perceptions
items.abstract: Process safety education is essential for preparing engineers to manage risks in high-hazard industries. In Algeria, process safety competencies are primarily addressed through Industrial Hygiene and Safety (HSI) programs, although no dedicated process safety specialization currently exists. This study evaluates Algerian HSI curricula through national curriculum mapping, a student perception survey, and benchmarking against the IChemE-accredited MSc Process Safety and Loss Prevention program at the University of Sheffield (UK) and the Master in Sécurité des Procédés Industriels, Environnement et Qualité (SPIEQ) at the University of Lorraine (French). The analysis shows that Algerian curricula provide broad coverage of risk assessment, fire and explosion safety, reliability, emergency management, and safety management. However, gaps remain in areas including inherently safer design, functional safety, human factors, and advanced process safety competencies. A survey of 42 students from the University of Laghouat indicates generally high satisfaction with the specialization, while also revealing concerns regarding assessment methods, language-related comprehension, and the connection between theoretical education and industrial practice. The findings highlight the need for a more competency-oriented curriculum, stronger university–industry collaboration, experiential learning, and greater integration of emerging digital technologies. This study provides an evidence-based framework to strengthen process safety education in Algeria and improve graduates’ preparedness for high-hazard industrial environments.

items.title: Identifying Barriers to the Safe Use of Artificial Intelligence in Emergency Clinical Decision-Making and Developing a Targeted Training Program for Emergency Physicians in Baghdad: A Mixed-Methods Study in a Private Hospital
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence tools are being deployed in emergency departments quicker than systems of governance, training and validation can put in place to ensure their safe use. There is practically no evidence on the barriers experienced by emergency medicine practitioners in Iraq and there is no developed curriculum for AI safety training for those working in this specialty. Objectives: The purpose of this study is to identify the barriers to safe application of AI in emergency clinical decision making encountered by doctors in a private clinic in Baghdad, and to develop, implement and assess training activities aimed at overcoming these barriers. Methods: The study was an institutional three-phase multi-method research conducted between January and July 2026 in the emergency department of a private tertiary care hospital in Baghdad. Phase 1 consisted of surveys using cross-sectional established questionnaire (census of all 84 eligible emergency medicine practitioners) complemented with 16 semi-structured interviews. Phase 2 was based on applying Kern’s six-step strategy to create a curriculum based on the barriers identified. Phase 3 included educational program assessment based on a single-group pre-post design at 1st and 2nd Kirkpatrick stages with an -week follow-up and measurements for the effect of automation bias. Results: Seventy-six doctors took part in the study (90.5%). Whereas 63.2% of doctors claimed having practical experience in working with AI technology, only 11.8% reported having received any formal training. The barriers were grouped into the domains rated highest: knowledge and skills gaps (4.12/5), legal and liability issues (3.98) and data constraints/validity (3.94). Prior training and digital literacy negatively correlated with the barrier score. Five qualitative themes emerged with the most important ones being trust issues. In the study with 39 participating physicians, the mean knowledge score rose from 9.8 on a scale of 20 to 15.6 (p < 0.001), while the percentage of errors detected was reported as increasing from 41.0% to 79.5%; on the other hand, the percentage of physicians inclined to accept incorrect AI recommendations fell from 51.3% to 17.9%. Nevertheless, results persisted after eight weeks. Major conclusions regarding the barriers preventing safe AI use in this field are that they basically relate to educational, regulatory and contextual issues rather than technological ones. A short, barrier-specific simulation-based intervention caused considerable progress of physicians’ ability to detect and override unsafe AI recommendations. items.title: Identity Without Disclosure: A Post-Centralized Authentication Architecture Using Decentralized Identifiers, Verifiable Credentials, and Zero-Knowledge Proofs
items.abstract: Contemporary digital identity systems are largely constructed around a disclosure-and-retention model: users disclose identifying information to a service provider, the provider stores that information in a centralized database, and subsequent authentication is used to recover access to the stored identity record. This architecture creates a structural contradiction. The more information an organization accumulates to establish trust, the more valuable that organization becomes as a target for compromise. This paper proposes a post-centralized identity architecture based on decentralized identifiers (DIDs), verifiable credentials (VCs), selective disclosure, and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs). Rather than repeatedly disclosing static personal information, individuals obtain cryptographically verifiable credentials from trusted issuers and present only the claims or predicates required for a specific transaction. A verifier may therefore confirm that a person is an adult, a resident of a jurisdiction, a licensed professional, or an authorized organizational representative without necessarily obtaining the underlying date of birth, address, license number, or other source data. The proposed architecture separates identity, authentication, authorization, and provenance, thereby reducing the value of centralized personal-data repositories while preserving institutional trust. It further extends provenance from creative artifacts to persons, organizations, artificial intelligence agents, and digitally mediated actions. The central argument is that privacy in an era of scalable cyberattack should shift from protecting ever-larger collections of personal data toward minimizing the creation of such collections in the first place.

items.title: ILM: An AI-Powered Storytelling Educational Tool
items.abstract: Digital technologies have made Islamic narratives more accessible, but existing platforms provide limited support for structured learning and comprehension of these stories, particularly in Arabic and multilingual settings. We present ILM, an interactive educational platform for Stories of the Prophets that combines Arabic natural language processing, structured knowledge representation, and retrieval-based question generation. Admin-approved Arabic narratives are processed by a Knowledge Graph (KG) Constructor Engine that identifies entities and narrative relationships and stores them as structured knowledge, enabling learners to explore stories through a visual story map and answer entity- and relation-based questions generated from the KG. Separately, a multilingual retrieval pipeline retrieves relevant passages from the original narratives to generate multiple-choice and open-ended comprehension questions. For open-ended questions, an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluates learners' answers against the retrieved passages and reference answers to determine correctness. The platform also incorporates Quranic content as a separate enrichment layer, allowing selected narratives to be supplemented with source-supported information. By combining structured knowledge with passage-based retrieval, ILM supports narrative exploration, comprehension, and assessment across Arabic and multilingual content. The system demonstrates the feasibility of combining structured knowledge representation and retrieval-based generation to support interactive learning of Islamic narratives. A demo is available at anonymous.4open.science/r/mml-5FCF.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Digital Library Services on Research and Academic Productivity
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming library services in higher education by enhancing information retrieval, recommendation, and access. AI systems improve search capabilities, offer research suggestions, provide reference assistance, and facilitate access to scholarly materials, thus helping students and faculty to remain productive. This article examines the impact of AI on digital library services and on academic productivity, drawing on selected studies. The literature includes topics such as resources, research productivity, AI adoption in academic libraries, AI literacy, and support services. Findings indicate that digital library resources significantly aid researchers in quickly locating information and enhancing retrieval efficiency. Studies suggest that AI strengthens library services by personalising experiences, expediting content discovery, increasing user engagement, and improving operational efficiency.The review concludes that AI-enabled digital library services could substantially boost research and academic productivity if supported by robust technical infrastructure, comprehensive training, professional guidance, and ethical standards.

items.title: Impacts of Edge AI/agentic AI on supply chain management and operations research
items.abstract: Abstract Edge AI refers to the deployment and execution of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms on decentralized, local computing devices (e.g., Internet of Things) rather than relying on centralized cloud‐based computing infrastructures. The literature has addressed the increasing importance of AI in supply chain and operations management (SCOM), specifically in learning‐based, generative, and agentic AI, as well as digital twins. However, the area of Edge AI has not yet received a theoretical framing and conceptualization in SCOM. In this paper, we discuss the impacts of Edge AI on SCOM. We begin with an analysis of AI in SCOM, focusing on learning‐based, generative, agentic AI, and digital twins. We then detail Edge AI's impacts on SCOM across Digital SCOR functions: orchestration, fulfillment and ordering, planning, sourcing, regeneration, synchronization, and transformation. We also analyze organizational transformations that Edge AI might trigger. Specifically, we discuss interactions of agentic AI and Edge AI, an integration of local and centralized decision‐making, and deployment scenarios of Edge AI use in SCOM, focusing on production planning and control, intralogistics, and supply chain resilience. Risks and challenges of the new technology are considered as well. Impacts of Edge AI on supply chain and operations research are discussed. We conclude that Edge AI is a crucial part of the unfolding Industry 6.0 revolution that, in combination with agentic AI, provides a technology to implement decentralized, autonomously planned and controlled supply chain, production, and logistics processes, materializing in Industry 6.0 with AI across all layers of value‐added chains.

items.title: IMPLEMENTASI MODEL PBL PADA MATA PELAJARAN IPS KELAS VIII DI SMP NEGERI 4 SAMARINDA
items.abstract: Social studies instruction in junior high schools is frequently dominated by conventional lecturing methods, resulting in low cognitive engagement and passive student involvement. This pedagogical gap necessitates the implementation of innovative learning models capable of contextualizing academic content with real-world societal phenomena. This study aims to describe the implementation of the Problem-Based Learning (PBL) model in eighth-grade social studies instruction at SMP Negeri 4 Samarinda and identify the operational obstacles encountered by both teachers and students. A qualitative descriptive approach was utilized with informants selected via purposive sampling, consisting of one certified social studies teacher and five students representing diverse academic performance levels. Data collection was carried out through passive participant observation, in-depth semi-structured interviews, and documentary review of teaching modules from August to October 2025. Data analysis followed the interactive model of Miles and Huberman, encompassing data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing, validated through source and methodological triangulation. The results reveal that PBL implementation proceeded through differentiated module planning, systematic execution of five PBL syntax phases supported by contextual audio-visual media on Indonesian geographical conditions, and authentic rubric-based assessment evaluating collaborative processes and final presentations. Key operational obstacles included restricted instructional time allocations, unstable school internet connectivity, unequal role distribution within group discussions, and limited classroom audio speaker facilities. ABSTRAK Praktik pembelajaran Ilmu Pengetahuan Sosial (IPS) di sekolah menengah pertama masih kerap didominasi oleh metode ceramah konvensional yang mengakibatkan rendahnya keterlibatan kognitif dan keaktifan kritis peserta didik. Kondisi kesenjangan pedagogis tersebut menuntut adanya implementasi model pembelajaran inovatif yang mampu mengontekstualisasikan materi pelajaran dengan fenomena riil kemasyarakatan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mendeskripsikan implementasi model Problem-Based Learning (PBL) dalam pembelajaran IPS kelas VIII-1 di SMP Negeri 4 Samarinda serta mengidentifikasi berbagai kendala operasional yang dihadapi guru dan peserta didik selama proses pembelajaran berlangsung. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan jenis deskriptif melalui pemilihan informan secara purposive sampling, yang melibatkan satu orang guru mata pelajaran IPS dan lima orang peserta didik berkemampuan variatif. Pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui observasi partisipatif pasif, wawancara mendalam semi-terstruktur, dan telaah dokumen modul ajar selama kurun waktu Agustus hingga Oktober 2025. Analisis data menerapkan model interaktif Miles dan Huberman yang meliputi kondensasi data, penyajian data, serta penarikan kesimpulan yang diuji keabsahannya melalui triangulasi sumber dan teknik. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa implementasi model PBL terlaksana melalui tahapan perencanaan modul ajar berdiferensiasi, pelaksanaan lima fase sintaks PBL terstruktur berbantuan media audio-visual kontekstual kondisi geografis Indonesia, serta evaluasi autentik berbasis rubrik proses dan kinerja. Kendala mendasar yang teridentifikasi mencakup keterbatasan alokasi jam pelajaran, ketidakstabilan jaringan internet sekolah, ketimpangan kontribusi peran dalam diskusi kelompok, serta keterbatasan perangkat pengeras suara ruang kelas.

items.title: Implementation of Statistical Quality Control (SQC) Method to Control the Quality of Refill Bodywash Packaging Products at PT. XYZ
items.abstract: General Background Quality control plays a vital role in liquid soap manufacturing to minimize defect rates and satisfy consumer expectations. Specific Background Refill liquid bodywash packaging lines encounter substantial quality deviations during manual filling and assembly processes. Knowledge Gap Existing research lacks quantitative diagnostic insights regarding root causes of defects in high-volume liquid packaging systems. Aims This investigation applies statistical quality control tools to systematically identify primary defect categories and underlying operational failure modes within a dedicated production line. Results Out of 60,792 total produced units, analysis reveals 1,574 defective packages, where untidy sealing accounts for 36% and tilted sealing represents 30% of total failures, alongside missing lot codes (29%) and leaks (5%). Statistical control charts indicate out-of-control conditions on days 6 and 10, while cause-and-effect diagrams link these errors to inadequate press maintenance, unstable sealing temperature, and operator fatigue. Novelty This work establishes empirical control thresholds and multi-factor cause mappings specifically tailored to manual refill packaging operations. Implications Implementing targeted machine maintenance schedules and operator ergonomics directly decreases defect occurrence and improves manufacturing yield. Key Findings Highlights Untidy and tilted sealing constitute 66% of all recorded packaging defects on the refill assembly line. Process stability analysis detects control limit breaches on specific production days due to operational parameters. Fishbone analysis traces defects to improper press temperatures, dirty sensors, and operator fatigue. Keywords Statistical Quality Control, Refill Packaging, Defect Reduction, Filling Assembly, Process Stability

Combined strategies achieved 100 percent of Team I targets, indicating the need for stronger communication and standardized partnerships.

items.title: Improving medication adherence through user experience: A qualitative study of smart pill box designs
items.abstract: Smart pill boxes are designed to support medication management, yet their value depends on how well they fit users' daily routines, abilities, and expectations. This qualitative study explored younger and older adults' user experience (UX) of smart pill boxes using Morville's User Experience Honeycomb model. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 30 participants, comprising 20 younger adults aged 18–49 years and 10 older adults aged 50 years or above. Thematic analysis was used to identify shared and age-specific concerns across the seven Honeycomb dimensions. The findings showed that both age groups valued smart pill boxes for practical medication management, especially reminders and help with organizing medication. Meanwhile, users described three recurring barriers. They found some devices burdensome to operate, insufficiently clear at the time of dosing, and difficult to fully trust when reliability or privacy was uncertain. Younger users tended to prefer flexible and connected functions, such as repeated or error reminders, refill support, and smartphone integration. In contrast, older users emphasized predictable operation, adequate compartment capacity, physical ease of use, and trust in storing medication in the device. Beyond these functional concerns, the device also provided perceived value by fostering habit formation, aiding medication planning, and promoting a sense of security. These findings suggest that smart pill boxes should not be designed merely as reminder devices, but as everyday medication-management tools that integrate digital alerts with trustworthy physical storage. Future designs should prioritize reliable core functions and layered interaction options to accommodate diverse user requirements across age groups.

items.title: In Silico Advertising Tests
items.abstract: This research examines whether large language model agents can produce analytically useful evidence for advertising testing when treated as synthetic respondents rather than as substitutes for human consumers. We report an in-silico comparative post-test of two television advertisements in the French telecommunications market, conducted on a panel of 800 profile-conditioned consumer agents. The study evaluates the synthetic corpus through internal validity criteria: whether the questionnaire covers the main dimensions of advertising response, whether evaluative dimensions form coherent relations, whether the two stimuli are discriminated across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic embeddings, and whether responses vary intelligibly across social profiles. The results indicate that the synthetic panel produces structured and interpretable evidence. The contribution is not that the analysis discovers a contrast invisible in the advertisements themselves: Bouygues and Orange are clearly built around different persuasive registers. Rather, the contribution is methodological. The synthetic-interview pipeline consistently recovers and differentiates these registers across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic comparisons. Bouygues is associated mainly with creative, humorous and memorable qualities, while Orange is associated with reliability, informativeness, purchase orientation and overall preference. This structure is visible quantitatively in the main six dimensional coding scheme. Among all 800 synthetic agents, Bouygues leads on creativity (83.6% versus 14.8% for Orange), whereas Orange leads on informationseeking or consideration (76.8% versus 14.8% for Bouygues) and overall preference (54.8% versus 20.6% for Bouygues), with the remaining responses classified as mixed or neutral. The analysis remains deliberately limited to synthetic respondents. Claims about similarity to human preferences or market behaviour would require external comparison with representative human data or market-level indicators.
